title: Want To Own A Tech Stock ETF? There's More Than The QQQ
detail:
Want To Own A Tech Stock ETF? There's More Than The QQQ
Andrew Legget
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 7:24 AM CDT 4 min read
QQQ
^IXIC
EMQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When it comes to broad tech exposure, many investors have focused their attention on the QQQ ETF, which provides exposure to the 100 largest, non-financial, companies on the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange.

And it makes a lot of sense. The names that dominate the Nasdaq are some of the biggest and most innovative tech stocks in the world.

However, while the companies that dominate the QQQ ETF may be great companies, the world of tech is wide.

What if you want to invest in tech stocks beyond the familiar names in Wall Street?

Why look beyond US tech stocks?

As great and as globally dominant as the U.S. tech giants are, they are not the only game in town.

Across emerging markets, a combination of large populations, growing consumer spending and expanding access to technology is creating opportunities for businesses beyond the usual Silicon Valley names.

As more people enter the online domain, demand for services such as online shopping, digital payments and internet-based platforms could rise alongside it.

In many of these markets, internet access as well as ownership of smartphones and computers is still in its infancy compared to developed markets. This means there is considerable opportunity for tech companies to develop solutions in markets where the US tech giants either have not already captured or have decided to skip.

Emerging markets rushing online

According to research from the International Technology Union (ITU), there is a significant disparity between internet usage between developed and emerging markets.

In 2024, the ITU estimated that around 93% of the population in high-income countries use the internet. This compares to just 27% of the population in low-income countries. However, while internet usage remains low, the rate of growth is significantly higher than the developed world at 8.5% compared to 3.4%.

Source: World Bank Group

This echoes data provided by the World Bank which reported that internet usage in lower-middle and low-income countries significantly lagged those of higher income countries. However, the total percentage of the population using the internet in these locations has been improving.

Source: World Bank Group

Specifically, the World Bank lists the South Asia region, which includes countries like India (amongst others), as being one of the fastest rising regions for internet usage, with Latin America, the Middle East and parts of Africa also showing significant internet adoption.

How to find emerging tech stocks in one place

The trend of increased adoption of the internet and technology in developed markets has not gone unnoticed.

Ask an average Joe what they know about exchange-traded funds and you'll probably get crickets. Mention QQQ and you might get a glimmer of recognition. The Nasdaq-100-tracking index fund has been around since 1999, and with more than $500 billion under management, it's one of the largest ETFs on the market.

"In all of that time, the options ecosystem has grown, the number of market makers, traders, how people use it has grown," said Brian Hartigan, Invesco's global head of ETFs and index investments. "It's grown up to become one of the most liquid and highly traded vehicles in the world."

Sign up for The Daily Upside at no cost for premium analysis on all your favorite stocks.

READ ALSO: Why Gold ETF Inflows Surged Even as the Metal's Price Fell and Getting a Little Defensive? Investors Tiptoe into Utilities, Low-Vol Funds

Late last month, Invesco launched its Nasdaq International Innovators 100 ETF (QQI), which tracks large- and mid-cap international companies. This addition to Invesco's Innovation Suite rounded out the product line to six ETFs, and Invesco isn't done. ETF Upside caught up with Hartigan to discuss what's next for the suite, innovations around the ETF wrapper and why they have no plans for golf partnerships any time soon.

You recently launched QQI, and you've got a couple other Q series funds in the works. What's next for the suite?

The US isn't the only innovative country in the world. Investors are probably underinvested in international as a whole, partly because of the way the US markets have run, but also just not-so-exciting returns or ways to allocate. So we think that's a good opportunity. In terms of how we expand, I think we'll continue to try to be ubiquitous in some ways with the Qs, and that's cross-listing, that's engaging globally with clients because some clients may want a UCITS or a London registered, and some may want the liquidity of a 'Q.' So continuing to promote Q as a whole, but starting to branch out with other Nasdaq listings and innovative listings across the globe.

Pulling the camera back to the wider ETF market, what do you think is going to be the next big development for ETFs, and how is it going to matter to investors and advisors?

Tokenization is interesting to the extent there's demand for it, but where we're looking at it is: What problem does it solve, or what utility does it create? Whether that's efficiency in the trading, if it's speed and settlements, if it's a new create/redeem mechanism that's quicker and frictionless, those are things that we're looking at just around ETFs. … The prediction markets are interesting, but I think that's more of a regulatory thing than it is an ETF thing. And private markets, same thing. There is a point at which everything doesn't have to be in an ETF. So almost stepping back to say 'ETFs, yes, they've continued to capture great new ideas and themes and ways for investors to invest, but I don't know that you know everything has to move its way through to an ETF, particularly if it doesn't make sense or adhere to the ETF core mechanics of pricing, transparency, and liquidity.'
